claim: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolved on earth about 2.5 billion years ago
source: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolved on earth about 2.5 billion years ago (Bekker, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bekker, 2004

claim: Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria carry out oxygenic photosynthesis
source: Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria carry out this process and are found in a wide variety of environments.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about which organisms perform oxygenic photosynthesis

claim: All oxygenic photosynthetic organisms use photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII) to convert solar energy to chemical energy
source: Despite nearly 3 billion years of evolution, all oxygenic photosynthetic organisms use the same large pigment–protein complexes, known as photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII), to convert solar energy to chemical energy (Fromme et al., 2003; Witt, 1996; Zouni et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature

claim: Both PSI and PSII use light to induce a charge separation event and transport high-energy electrons
source: Both complexes use light to induce a charge separation event, then transport the high-energy electron, ultimately to be stored as a chemical bond (Fromme et al., 2003; Witt, 1996; Zouni et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature

claim: Excess light can damage photosynthetic proteins in a process called photoinhibition
source: Although light is required for photosynthesis, an excess of light can be detrimental to photosynthetic organisms by damaging the photosynthetic proteins in a process called photoinhibition (Kok, 1956; Jones and Kok, 1966; Gururani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature

claim: Photoprotective mechanisms include changes in photosystem content
source: To prevent photoinhibition, photoprotective mechanisms such as changes in the photosystem content (Muramatsu and Hihara, 2012; Murakami and Fujita, 1991; Demmig-Adams and Adams, 1992; Miskiewicz et al., 2002), dissipation of excess energy as heat (Peltier and Schmidt, 1991; Levy et al., 1993; Jacob and Lawlor, 1993), and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes have been observed (Tsang et al., 1991; Camp, 1994; Zhang and Scheller, 2004; Ort and Baker, 2002; Horling, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations

claim: Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 decreases the PSI:PSII ratio in response to high light
source: A response shown by the model cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 to high light is to decrease the PSI:PSII ratio, minimizing its light harvesting capacity and presumably protecting against the generation of reactive oxygen species around PSI (Hihara et al., 1998; Sonoike et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature

claim: Vascular plants decrease PSI:PSII ratio in response to high light
source: This is in agreement with the response observed in vascular plants (Anderson, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation

claim: Synechococcus OS-B' increases the PSI:PSII ratio upon high-light conditions
source: In the terrestrial cyanobacteria, Synechococcus OS-B', isolated from a microbial mat in a hot spring, the ratio of PSI:PSII increases upon high-light conditions (Kilian, 2007), demonstrating the importance of PSI in the high-light response of cyanobacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation

claim: PSI-specific damage is irreversible and long lived due to a lack of repair mechanisms
source: PSI-specific damage, however, is irreversible and long lived due to a lack of repair mechanisms, requiring the biosynthesis of new PSI polypeptides (Li et al., 2004; Sonoike, 2010; Terashima et al., 1994; Sonoike et al., 1995; Lima-Melo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations

claim: Fluctuating light and low temperatures cause PSI photoinhibition by causing an imbalance in the redox state of PSI donors and acceptors
source: Fluctuating light and low temperatures have been attributed to PSI photoinhibition by causing an imbalance in the redox state of PSI donors and acceptors (Sonoike, 2010; Allahverdiyeva et al., 2015; Tiwari, 2016; Kudoh and Sonoike, 2002; Kono and Terashima, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations

claim: Recovery times in leaves for PSI-specific photodamage are longer than a week
source: Recovery times in leaves for PSI-specific photodamage have been reported to be longer than a week, much longer than the 30 min half-life of the D1 protein of PSII (Zhang and Scheller, 2004; Yao et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2004; Kudoh and Sonoike, 2002; Zhou et al., 2004; Kanervo et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations

claim: The D1 protein of PSII has a 30 min half-life
source: Recovery times in leaves for PSI-specific photodamage have been reported to be longer than a week, much longer than the 30 min half-life of the D1 protein of PSII (Zhang and Scheller, 2004; Yao et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2004; Kudoh and Sonoike, 2002; Zhou et al., 2004; Kanervo et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: PSI inhibition results in the over-reduction of the plastoquinone pool subsequently inhibiting PSII
source: PSI inhibition is therefore potentially more devastating than damage to PSII because it results in the over-reduction of the plastoquinone pool subsequently inhibiting PSII and thereby blocking the complete electron transfer chain (Sonoike, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation

claim: Photoinhibition of PSII is a mechanism to protect PSI by reducing the amount of electrons sent to PSI
source: This has lead to the proposal that photoinhibition of PSII is a mechanism to protect PSI by reducing the amount of electrons sent to PSI (Barbato et al., 2020; Tikkanen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: Cyanobacterial PSI has a core antenna system comprised of 96 chlorophyll a molecules
source: The first high-resolution structure of cyanobacterial PSI revealed a core antenna system comprised of 96 chlorophyll a (Chla) molecules, of which 6 are integral to the electron transport chain (ETC), while the remaining chlorophyll molecules function to harvest light and transfer excitation energy to the ETC (Fromme et al., 2006; Jordan et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies

claim: Six chlorophyll a molecules are integral to the electron transport chain in cyanobacterial PSI
source: The first high-resolution structure of cyanobacterial PSI revealed a core antenna system comprised of 96 chlorophyll a (Chla) molecules, of which 6 are integral to the electron transport chain (ETC), while the remaining chlorophyll molecules function to harvest light and transfer excitation energy to the ETC (Fromme et al., 2006; Jordan et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies

claim: One Chla of P700 is Chla', the C13 epimer of Chla
source: While all chlorophyll molecules in cyanobacteria are chemically identical except one (one Chla of P700 is Chla', the C13 epimer of Chla), the local environment of a few individual chlorophylls has been shown to extend their absorbance properties above 700 nm, giving rise to long-wavelength chlorophylls (LWC) (Fromme et al., 2006; Wientjes et al., 2012; Croce and van Amerongen, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: The local environment of a few individual chlorophylls extends their absorbance properties above 700 nm, giving rise to long-wavelength chlorophylls (LWC)
source: While all chlorophyll molecules in cyanobacteria are chemically identical except one (one Chla of P700 is Chla', the C13 epimer of Chla), the local environment of a few individual chlorophylls has been shown to extend their absorbance properties above 700 nm, giving rise to long-wavelength chlorophylls (LWC) (Fromme et al., 2006; Wientjes et al., 2012; Croce and van Amerongen, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: In cyanobacteria, LWC are associated with PSI
source: Further studies have revealed that, in cyanobacteria, LWC are associated with PSI and the amount of these pigments vary between species, suggesting that the number of LWC is an important evolutionary adaptation (Shubin et al., 1991; Gobets et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: The amount of LWC varies between cyanobacterial species
source: Further studies have revealed that, in cyanobacteria, LWC are associated with PSI and the amount of these pigments vary between species, suggesting that the number of LWC is an important evolutionary adaptation (Shubin et al., 1991; Gobets et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: The absorbance properties of specific chlorophylls are highly dependent on coordinating residues and excitonic coupling between neighboring chlorophylls
source: The absorbance properties of specific chlorophylls are highly dependent on its coordinating residues as well as excitonic coupling between neighboring chlorophylls; and changing either can alter the spectroscopic properties of a chlorophyll. (Wientjes et al., 2011; Toporik, 2020; Khmelnitskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: Higher plants exclusively utilize monomeric PSI
source: Higher plants exclusively utilize monomeric PSI, whereas cyanobacteria utilize monomeric, trimeric, and tetrameric oligomers (Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: Cyanobacteria utilize monomeric, trimeric, and tetrameric PSI oligomers
source: Higher plants exclusively utilize monomeric PSI, whereas cyanobacteria utilize monomeric, trimeric, and tetrameric oligomers (Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: The PsaL subunit is vital for PSI oligomeric complexes to form
source: The PsaL subunit has been shown to be vital for these larger oligomeric complexes to form (Li et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2019; Chitnis and Chitnis, 1993; Malavath et al., 2018).

claim: Adding a single histidine to the C-terminus of PsaL completely disrupts trimerization in Synechocystis
source: Adding a single histidine to the C-terminus of PsaL was shown to completely disrupt trimerization in Synechocystis (Malavath et al., 2018; Netzer-El et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations

claim: The C-terminus of PsaL coordinates a calcium ion together with the PsaL subunit of the adjacent monomer in PSI structures from Thermosynechococcus elongatus and Synechocystis sp. PCC. 6,803
source: The first crystal structures of PSI from Thermosynechococcus elongatus and Synechocystis sp. PCC. 6,803 (Synechocystis) showed that the C-terminus of PsaL coordinates a calcium ion together with the PsaL subunit of the adjacent monomer, which was suggested to stabilize trimer formation and emphasized the importance of the C-terminus of PsaL in oligomerization (Jordan et al., 2001; Mazor et al., 2013).
